cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: FX swaps and cross-currency swaps are both used principally to manage long-term interest rate risk rather than funding needs.
cards.explanation: FX swaps are short-dated funding and liquidity instruments, not tools for long-term interest rate management.
cards.originalText: Both are used principally to manage long-term interest rate risk rather than funding needs.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: FX swaps and cross-currency swaps are both transacted principally by central banks in the management of foreign currency reserves.
cards.explanation: Although central banks use FX swaps (for example crisis-era swap lines), both instruments are overwhelmingly used by commercial banks and corporates.
cards.originalText: Both are transacted principally by central banks in the management of foreign currency reserves.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: An FX swap used to fund a five-year asset would carry no rollover risk over the five years, because the far leg rate is fixed at inception and can be extended on the same terms.
cards.explanation: FX swaps are short dated, so funding a five-year asset requires repeated rollover, and there is no right to extend on the original terms.
cards.originalText: An FX swap would carry no rollover risk over the five years, because the far leg rate is fixed at inception and can be extended on the same terms.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: Under a cross-currency swap the parties exchange principal at inception and re-exchange at maturity, and each pays interest on the currency it received during the life of the trade.
cards.explanation: In a cross-currency swap principal is exchanged at inception, each party pays periodic interest on the currency it received, and principal is re-exchanged at maturity, normally at the original spot rate.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: An FX swap expresses the interest rate differential through periodic payments, while a cross-currency swap embeds it in the forward rate.
cards.explanation: It is the reverse: an FX swap embeds the interest differential in the forward rate, while a cross-currency swap expresses it through periodic interest payments.
cards.correction: A cross-currency swap expresses the interest rate differential through periodic payments, while an FX swap embeds it in the forward rate.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk

cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: A cross-currency swap expresses the interest rate differential through periodic payments, while an FX swap embeds it in the forward rate.
cards.explanation: It is the reverse: an FX swap embeds the interest differential in the forward rate, while a cross-currency swap expresses it through periodic interest payments.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: The cross-currency basis is the difference between the spot and forward rates on an FX swap, and it is zero whenever covered interest parity holds.
cards.explanation: The cross-currency basis is the spread applied to one leg of a cross-currency swap to equalise the value of the two legs, not the spot-to-forward difference on an FX swap.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: Post-crisis regulatory change has expanded the scope for speculative proprietary trading by US banks, increasing the capital devoted to closing the cross-currency basis.
cards.explanation: Post-crisis rules such as the Volcker rule and higher capital requirements reduced the capital available for proprietary trading; less arbitrage capital is part of why the basis persists.
cards.originalText: Regulatory change has expanded the scope for speculative proprietary trading by US banks, increasing the capital devoted to closing the basis.
cards.correction: Post-crisis regulatory change has reduced the scope for speculative proprietary trading by US banks, reducing the capital devoted to closing the cross-currency basis.

cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost

cards.explanation: Post-crisis rules such as the Volcker rule and higher capital requirements reduced the capital available for proprietary trading; less arbitrage capital is part of why the basis persists.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: Given the general decline in global interest rates, the inclusion of a liquidity risk cost in swap pricing is no longer necessary.
cards.explanation: Liquidity and funding risk costs became more significant in swap pricing after the crisis, and the level of interest rates does not determine whether such a cost is warranted.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: The cross-currency basis increasingly incorporates the financing and balance sheet costs incurred by arbitrageurs in maintaining the positions that would otherwise close it.
cards.explanation: Covered interest parity holds only while arbitrage is costless; since 2008 balance sheet constraints have made the arbitrage costly, so a non-zero basis persists.
cards.originalText: The basis increasingly incorporates the financing and balance sheet costs incurred by arbitrageurs in maintaining the positions that would otherwise close it.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: Deviations from covered interest parity are largest at quarter and year ends, because banks reduce balance sheet usage for regulatory reporting dates, which withdraws precisely the capacity the arbitrage requires.
cards.explanation: Deviations spike around reporting dates as banks shrink balance sheets, which identifies balance sheet capacity as the binding constraint on CIP arbitrage.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: Deviations from covered interest parity are largest in the most liquid currency pairs, since high turnover makes the basis more volatile and therefore wider on average.
cards.explanation: Deviations are widest where structural dollar funding demand is greatest and balance sheet is scarcest; liquidity tends to narrow a basis rather than widen it.
cards.originalText: Deviations are largest in the most liquid currency pairs, since high turnover makes the basis more volatile and therefore wider on average.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: The persistence of the cross-currency basis indicates a straightforward unexploited arbitrage, and its size measures the risk-free profit available to any institution willing to take the trade.
cards.explanation: The basis approximates the cost of carrying the arbitrage position (balance sheet and financing costs), so it is not a risk-free profit.
cards.originalText: The persistence of the basis indicates a straightforward unexploited arbitrage, and its size measures the risk-free profit available to any institution willing to take the trade.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
cards.statement: Because covered interest parity is a no-arbitrage identity derived from spot and forward rates alone, a non-zero basis can only reflect an error in the quoted forward rate.
cards.explanation: Covered interest parity involves spot and forward rates and the two interest rates, and holds only if arbitrage is costless and unconstrained; the cost of arbitrage, not quotation error, explains the basis.

cards.statement: A bankers' acceptance is a bank's commitment to pay a stated sum on a stated future date under stated conditions, and one disadvantage is that it cannot be traded before maturity.

cards.explanation: Because supply is driven by underlying trade transactions, acceptances come in odd denominations and are not available in every maturity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: The risk that a bank must sell part of its investment portfolio before maturity and realise a capital loss is prepayment risk.
cards.explanation: Selling before maturity at a loss is liquidity risk; prepayment risk concerns early repayment by the borrowers behind a security.
cards.originalText: The risk that the bank must sell part of its portfolio before maturity and realise a capital loss is prepayment risk.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: The risk that loans pooled as collateral behind a security are repaid ahead of schedule, which is particularly acute for residential mortgages, is call risk.
cards.explanation: Early repayment of pooled loans (acute for residential mortgages) is prepayment risk; call risk is the issuer's contractual right to redeem the security early.
cards.correction: The risk that loans pooled as collateral behind a security are repaid ahead of schedule, which is particularly acute for residential mortgages, is prepayment risk.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: The risk that loans pooled as collateral behind a security are repaid ahead of schedule, which is particularly acute for residential mortgages, is prepayment risk.
cards.explanation: Early repayment of pooled loans (acute for residential mortgages) is prepayment risk; call risk is the issuer's contractual right to redeem the security early.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: The risk that a bank must sell part of its investment portfolio before maturity and realise a capital loss is liquidity risk.
cards.explanation: In the context of bank investment securities, liquidity risk is the risk of a forced sale before maturity at a capital loss.
cards.originalText: The risk that the bank must sell part of its portfolio before maturity and realise a capital loss is liquidity risk.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: The risk that rising prices for goods and services erode the purchasing power of interest income and repaid principal is business risk.
cards.explanation: Erosion of purchasing power by rising prices is inflation risk; business risk concerns deterioration in the local economy the bank serves.
cards.correction: The risk that rising prices for goods and services erode the purchasing power of interest income and repaid principal is inflation risk.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: The risk that rising prices for goods and services erode the purchasing power of interest income and repaid principal is inflation risk.
cards.explanation: Erosion of purchasing power by rising prices is inflation risk; business risk concerns deterioration in the local economy the bank serves.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: The requirement that a bank post acceptable securities as backing before it can accept deposits from federal, state and local government units is a pledging requirement, which constrains the composition of the investment portfolio because only certain securities qualify as acceptable collateral.
cards.explanation: Pledging requirements safeguard public funds; the bank must hold qualifying securities (typically Treasury and agency paper), and pledged securities are encumbered.
cards.originalText: Pledging requirements, which constrain the composition of the portfolio because only certain securities qualify as acceptable collateral.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: A tax swap realises a loss to offset taxable income while leaving the portfolio's risk and maturity profile substantially unchanged.
cards.explanation: A tax swap sells securities with an unrealised loss and reinvests in similar instruments, so the loss is deductible against current income while the economic position is largely preserved.
cards.originalText: A tax swap, which realises a loss to offset taxable income while leaving the portfolio's risk and maturity profile substantially unchanged.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: Portfolio immunisation protects the realised return on the portfolio against movements in interest rates.
cards.explanation: Immunisation matches portfolio duration to the planning horizon to protect the realised return from rate movements; it has no tax objective.
cards.originalText: Portfolio immunisation, which protects the realised return on the portfolio against movements in interest rates.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: A rate expectation strategy shifts the maturity structure of the portfolio in anticipation of a change in interest rates.
cards.explanation: A rate expectation strategy repositions maturities based on an interest rate forecast.
cards.originalText: A rate expectation strategy, which shifts the maturity structure of the portfolio in anticipation of a change in interest rates.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: The barbell strategy is the most aggressive approach, requiring the bank to shift maturities continually in response to interest rate forecasts.
cards.explanation: The barbell is a structural allocation to both ends of the maturity spectrum; the most aggressive approach, which shifts maturities on rate forecasts, is the rate expectation strategy.
cards.correction: The rate expectation strategy is the most aggressive approach, requiring the bank to shift maturities continually in response to interest rate forecasts.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: The rate expectation strategy is the most aggressive approach, requiring the bank to shift maturities continually in response to interest rate forecasts.
cards.explanation: The barbell is a structural allocation to both ends of the maturity spectrum; the most aggressive approach, which shifts maturities on rate forecasts, is the rate expectation strategy.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: The rate expectation strategy is the most aggressive bank investment maturity strategy, requiring the bank to shift the maturities of its securities continually in response to forecast changes in interest rates.
cards.explanation: The rate expectation strategy's success depends entirely on forecasting accuracy, which makes it the most aggressive of the maturity management approaches.
cards.originalText: The rate expectation strategy is the most aggressive approach, requiring the bank to shift the maturities of its securities continually in response to forecast changes in interest rates.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: Portfolio immunisation protects the bank against credit deterioration in the securities held, regardless of the direction of interest rates.
cards.explanation: Immunisation protects against interest rate movements, not credit deterioration, which is a separate risk requiring separate management.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: A front-end load maturity policy places the portfolio predominantly in long-dated securities, which maximises income while sacrificing liquidity.
cards.explanation: A front-end load policy concentrates holdings at the short end and emphasises liquidity; concentrating in long-dated securities is the back-end load policy.
cards.correction: A back-end load maturity policy places the portfolio predominantly in long-dated securities, which maximises income while sacrificing liquidity.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
cards.statement: A back-end load maturity policy places the portfolio predominantly in long-dated securities, which maximises income while sacrificing liquidity.
cards.explanation: A front-end load policy concentrates holdings at the short end and emphasises liquidity; concentrating in long-dated securities is the back-end load policy.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
cards.statement: Client intraday credit usage compares a client's peak daily intraday overdraft against the credit line established for that client.
cards.explanation: Client intraday credit usage measures the client's position against the line the bank extended to it, distinct from the bank's own peak usage.
cards.originalText: Client intraday credit usage.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
cards.statement: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage compares a client's peak daily intraday overdraft against the credit line established for that client.
cards.explanation: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage measures the bank's own largest net negative position during the day; comparing a client's peak overdraft to its line is client intraday credit usage.
cards.originalText: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
cards.statement: The settlement positions measure monitors a bank's intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at every financial market utility in which it participates, capturing transaction-level detail wherever possible for later analysis.
cards.explanation: No measure called settlement positions exists in the reading. Tracking intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at every financial market utility, at transaction level, is the definition of the other cash transactions measure, one of the measures for understanding intraday flows.
cards.originalText: Settlement positions.
cards.correction: The other cash transactions measure monitors a bank's intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at every financial market utility in which it participates, capturing transaction-level detail wherever possible for later analysis.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
cards.statement: The other cash transactions measure monitors a bank's intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at every financial market utility in which it participates, capturing transaction-level detail wherever possible for later analysis.
cards.explanation: Tracking intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at every financial market utility, capturing transaction-level detail for analysis, is how the reading defines the other cash transactions measure for understanding intraday flows.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: A dealer bank intermediates between issuers and investors in the primary market, and between sellers and buyers of already issued securities in the secondary market.
cards.explanation: The primary market is where securities are issued for the first time (underwriting and distribution); the secondary market is where existing securities change hands (market making).
cards.originalText: In the primary market it intermediates between issuers and investors, and in the secondary market between sellers and buyers of already issued securities.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: A dealer bank intermediates between sellers and buyers of already issued securities in the primary market, and between issuers and investors in the secondary market.
cards.explanation: The two markets are transposed: new issuance, intermediating between issuers and investors, is by definition the primary market.
cards.originalText: In the primary market it intermediates between sellers and buyers of already issued securities, and in the secondary market between issuers and investors.
cards.correction: A dealer bank intermediates between sellers and buyers of already issued securities in the secondary market, and between issuers and investors in the primary market.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: A dealer bank intermediates between sellers and buyers of already issued securities in the secondary market, and between issuers and investors in the primary market.
cards.explanation: The two markets are transposed: new issuance, intermediating between issuers and investors, is by definition the primary market.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: A dealer bank intermediates exclusively between other dealer banks in both the primary and secondary markets, since retail and institutional clients access the market through separate channels.
cards.explanation: Dealer banks intermediate for issuers, institutional investors, corporates and other dealers alike; the interdealer market is only one segment.
cards.originalText: In both markets it intermediates exclusively between other dealer banks, since retail and institutional clients access the market through separate channels.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Over-the-counter trades are negotiated publicly on an exchange, and a dealer's primary source of profit on them is the commission charged on each transaction.
cards.explanation: OTC trades are negotiated privately between two counterparties, and the dealer's return is embedded in the bid-offer spread rather than charged as a commission.
cards.originalText: Over-the-counter trades are negotiated publicly on an exchange, and the dealer's primary source of profit is the commission charged on each transaction.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Over-the-counter trades are negotiated privately between the two counterparties, and a dealer's primary source of profit on them is the difference between its bid and offer terms.
cards.explanation: Dealers aim to run a matched book and earn the bid-offer spread rather than a directional return.
cards.originalText: Over-the-counter trades are negotiated privately between the two counterparties, and the dealer's primary source of profit is the difference between its bid and offer terms.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Over-the-counter trades are negotiated privately, and a dealer's primary source of profit on them is the appreciation in value of the underlying instruments it holds outright.
cards.explanation: That describes a proprietary trading return; a dealer's core derivatives profit is the bid-offer spread, and a matched book minimises directional exposure.
cards.originalText: Over-the-counter trades are negotiated privately, and the dealer's primary source of profit is the appreciation in value of the underlying instruments it holds outright.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Over-the-counter trades are negotiated privately, and dealer banks hold predominantly exchange-traded futures because these carry no counterparty exposure.
cards.explanation: Interest rate swaps, which are OTC and do carry counterparty exposure, are the most widely held derivative among banks.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: In a repurchase agreement, the haircut is a form of risk mitigation, requiring collateral worth more than the cash advanced so that the lender is protected against a fall in collateral value.
cards.explanation: Cash advanced equals collateral value times (1 minus the haircut), so the haircut is over-collateralisation that cushions the cash lender.
cards.originalText: It is a form of risk mitigation, requiring collateral worth more than the cash advanced so that the lender is protected against a fall in collateral value.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: In a repurchase agreement, the haircut is a reduction in the return earned by the cash lender, applied when the collateral is of higher quality than the market standard.
cards.explanation: The return on a repo is the repo rate; the haircut is a quantity of excess collateral, and higher quality collateral attracts a smaller haircut.
cards.originalText: It is a reduction in the return earned by the cash lender, applied when the collateral is of higher quality than the market standard.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: In a repurchase agreement, the haircut is an increase in the return earned by the cash lender, compensating for the illiquidity of the collateral pledged.
cards.explanation: The haircut is not a return adjustment; it is excess collateral protecting the lender, and any compensation would come through the repo rate.
cards.originalText: It is an increase in the return earned by the cash lender, compensating for the illiquidity of the collateral pledged.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: The haircut is a term used only in securities lending transactions and has no application in repurchase agreements.
cards.explanation: Haircuts are central to repurchase agreements and are the main channel through which repo funding tightens in a stress.
cards.originalText: It is a term used only in securities lending transactions and has no application in repurchase agreements.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: The flight of short-term creditors, who decline to roll over a dealer's repo and commercial paper funding, is a recognised mechanism through which a large dealer bank comes under terminal stress.
cards.explanation: Flight of short-term creditors is the primary and fastest-acting failure channel: funding must be replaced daily and refusal to roll forces immediate asset sales.
cards.originalText: The flight of short-term creditors, who decline to roll over the dealer's repo and commercial paper funding.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: The departure of prime brokerage clients, who move their balances and collateral to other dealers, is a recognised mechanism through which a large dealer bank comes under terminal stress.
cards.explanation: Prime brokerage client departures remove both free credit balances and rehypothecable collateral, which had been a cheap funding source.
cards.originalText: The departure of prime brokerage clients, who move their balances and collateral to other dealers.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Cash-draining actions by derivatives counterparties seeking to reduce their exposures to a dealer are a recognised mechanism through which a large dealer bank comes under terminal stress.
cards.explanation: Derivatives counterparties drain cash through collateral calls, novations and terminations.
cards.originalText: Cash-draining actions by derivatives counterparties seeking to reduce their exposures to the dealer.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: The extension of additional clearing-bank privileges, which increases a dealer's intraday credit capacity, is a recognised mechanism through which a large dealer bank comes under terminal stress.
cards.explanation: Additional clearing-bank privileges expand a dealer's capacity; it is the withdrawal of clearing-bank credit that is a failure mechanism.
cards.originalText: The extension of additional clearing-bank privileges, which increases the dealer's intraday credit capacity.
cards.correction: The extension of additional clearing-bank privileges, which increases a dealer's intraday credit capacity, is not a recognised mechanism through which a large dealer bank comes under terminal stress.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: The extension of additional clearing-bank privileges, which increases a dealer's intraday credit capacity, is not a recognised mechanism through which a large dealer bank comes under terminal stress.
cards.explanation: Additional clearing-bank privileges expand a dealer's capacity; it is the withdrawal of clearing-bank credit that is a failure mechanism.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Regulatory supervision together with risk-based capital requirements, which reduce the likelihood of a solvency-threatening capital loss, is a standard policy tool for addressing the social costs of bank failures.
cards.explanation: Supervision and capital requirements act before failure by reducing the probability that losses exhaust capital.
cards.originalText: Regulatory supervision together with risk-based capital requirements, which reduce the likelihood of a solvency-threatening capital loss.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Deposit insurance, which protects depositors and thereby removes their incentive to run, is a standard policy tool for addressing the social costs of bank failures.
cards.explanation: Deposit insurance removes the depositor's incentive to run, the classic failure channel for a commercial bank.
cards.originalText: Deposit insurance, which protects depositors and thereby removes their incentive to run.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Regulatory resolution mechanisms, which give the authorities powers to liquidate or restructure a failing bank in an orderly way, are a standard policy tool for addressing the social costs of bank failures.
cards.explanation: Resolution mechanisms act after failure, allowing orderly liquidation or restructuring rather than disorderly collapse.
cards.originalText: Regulatory resolution mechanisms, which give the authorities powers to liquidate or restructure a failing bank in an orderly way.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Regulatory requirements governing the departure of prime brokerage customers from a distressed dealer are a standard policy tool for addressing the social costs of bank failures.
cards.explanation: No standard policy tool governs the departure of prime brokerage customers, which is why dealer bank failures are hard to address with the existing toolkit built around deposit-funded banks.
cards.originalText: Regulatory requirements governing the departure of prime brokerage customers from a distressed dealer.
cards.correction: Regulatory requirements governing the departure of prime brokerage customers from a distressed dealer are not a standard policy tool for addressing the social costs of bank failures.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Regulatory requirements governing the departure of prime brokerage customers from a distressed dealer are not a standard policy tool for addressing the social costs of bank failures.
cards.explanation: No standard policy tool governs the departure of prime brokerage customers, which is why dealer bank failures are hard to address with the existing toolkit built around deposit-funded banks.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: For a dealer bank whose over-the-counter counterparties are rapidly reducing their exposures, the action most likely to regain their confidence is continuing to accept all trades with counterparties on the terms prevailing in the market, demonstrating that it remains an ordinary participant.
cards.explanation: A run on a dealer is driven by information; trading normally on market terms directly contradicts the market's hypothesis of impairment, whereas any deviation confirms the suspicion.
cards.originalText: Continuing to accept all trades with counterparties on the terms prevailing in the market, demonstrating that it remains an ordinary participant.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: For a dealer bank whose over-the-counter counterparties are rapidly reducing their exposures, the action most likely to regain their confidence is increasing its reliance on short-term borrowing to fund the resulting cash outflows.
cards.explanation: More short-term borrowing signals urgency and increases the amount that must be renewed each day, worsening the rollover exposure that makes dealers vulnerable.
cards.originalText: Increasing its reliance on short-term borrowing to fund the resulting cash outflows.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: An expectation of government support for institutions regarded as too big to fail encourages those institutions to take on more inefficient risk, because the cost of failure is not fully borne by them or their creditors.
cards.explanation: Expected support shifts the cost of failure away from the institution and its creditors, so creditors do not demand a funding cost that rises with risk, encouraging inefficient risk taking.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: An expectation of government support reduces risk taking at large dealer banks, since the implied guarantee lowers their funding costs and removes the need to reach for return.
cards.explanation: Lower funding costs from an implied guarantee are the channel of the distortion: creditors who expect protection do not discipline the borrower, so risk taking increases.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Because dealer banks fail through the withdrawal of short-term funding rather than through credit losses, higher capital requirements are the single sufficient policy response.
cards.explanation: Capital addresses solvency, whereas dealer banks fail through the withdrawal of short-term funding, a liquidity and confidence channel, so capital alone is not sufficient.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Assess policy measures that can alleviate firm-specific and systemic risks related to large dealer banks.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
cards.statement: Resolution regimes address the social costs of failure but cannot reduce moral hazard, since the expectation of support depends on institution size rather than on how failure is handled.
cards.explanation: A credible resolution regime reduces the expectation of government support, and it is that expectation, not size itself, that generates moral hazard.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 11: Contingency Funding Planning
cards.statement: The contingency funding plan should use scenarios developed independently of the liquidity stress testing framework, so that the two provide genuinely separate views of the bank's vulnerabilities.
cards.explanation: The contingency funding plan's scenarios should be aligned with those of the liquidity stress testing framework; otherwise the plan would be sized against events the stress test never measured.

cards.subject: Liquidity Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
cards.reading: LR2025, Ch. 11: Contingency Funding Planning
cards.statement: The contingency funding plan's stress scenarios should be aligned with those in the liquidity stress testing framework and with those used in recovery and resolution planning, and should cover both systemic and institution-specific risks.
cards.explanation: The stress test sizes the shortfall and the plan says what to do about it, so both must use a common scenario set, aligned also with recovery and resolution planning and covering systemic and idiosyncratic risks.
